newsitem.title: UK: First N.Ireland TV debate highlights age-old gulf.
newsitem.headline: First N.Ireland TV debate highlights age-old gulf.

text.p: Northern Ireland's key political adversaries battled each other inconclusively in a televised debate on Tuesday, three weeks before they are due to begin negotiating a lasting peace.

Neither Ken Maginnis of the Protestant Ulster Unionist Party nor Martin McGuinness of Sinn Fein, the IRA's political wing, showed any sign of softening the positions which have kept them apart for three decades.

Maginnis, security spokesman for the UUP, the province's main Protestant pro-British organisation, accused McGuinness of Catholic-backed Sinn Fein of being a leader of Irish Republican Army (IRA) guerrillas.
He opened the debate by stating: "I am being asked now to sit down with the leader of the IRA, with Martin McGuinness who has been Chief of Staff, who is the Godfather of Godfathers."
McGuinness, whose party shares the IRA goal of ending British rule of Northern Ireland to merge the province with the Irish republic, responded: "I reject absolutely what Ken Maginnis has said."
McGuinness, elected to the British parliament in May, is frequently accused by unionists of being a leader of Europe's most formidable guerrilla army.
He admitted that he was twice convicted of IRA membership in the Irish republic in his youth but said "that's rubbish" when accused by Maginnis of leading the IRA in his native Londonderry.

It was the first time the two men had appeared on British television together and marked an about turn for the UUP, which has yet to decide whether it will take part in peace talks with Sinn Fein starting in September.

But neither side showed any sign of softening their diametrically opposed views on what a peace settlement should consist of, who should vote on it and in what circumstances the negotiations should take place.
Maginnis demanded that the IRA agree to surrender some weapons during the negotiations to prove a commitment to democracy and to show that its war against Britain was over for good.

McGuinness countered that Sinn Fein "wants all the guns out of Irish politics" but said the British army, Northern Ireland police and rival Protestant loyalist extremists should all be disarmed at the same time.
His arguments were a re-run of Sinn Fein's longstanding demand that the talks focus on the "demilitarisation" of Northern Ireland prior to its merger with the Irish republic.

Britain says that weapons held by guerrillas cannot be equated with those held by 17,000 troops and 12,000 armed police and has voiced the hope that the IRA will agree to disarm during the talks, which are scheduled to end next May.

Sinn Fein will only be admitted to the negotiations if the IRA's July 20 ceasefire is deemed genuine by Britain but Maginnis gave no hint as to whether his party would take part in talks with Sinn Fein.

Britain and Ireland, co-sponsors of the talks, say Northern Ireland's British status will only change when a majority of people in the province, which is currently 60 per cent Protestant and 40 percent Catholic, want it.

Maginnis challenged McGuinness repeatedly in the 30-minute debate to accept the "principle of consent" which has been adopted by Britain, Ireland, the United States and talks chairman George Mitchell, a former U.S. senator.
McGuinness said: "Yes, we need the consent of everybody" but made clear he meant that any vote should also include the 3.5 million people of the Irish republic to the south.
The talks agenda includes proposals for a local assembly and cross-border bodies to oversee trade and local matters but McGuinness said he wanted to negotiate an end to British rule.
"What we have to do is to recognise that this Northern state has failed," he said. "Everything will be on the table, including the Union (with Britain)," he said.
